Although Gerald did not make landfall in Taiwan, it came close enough to deliver heavy rains and strong winds to the island. Five people were killed. Two young boys died due to flash flooding in the capital of Taipei. A worker at a nuclear power plant in the southern tip of the island died due to head injuries suffered during the storm. Two fishermen near Hualien drowned due to storm surge. Overall, five people were killed.[11]

Typhoon Gerald brought up to 510 mm of rain to the Fujian Province, with the cities of Ningde, Fuzhou, Putian, Quanzhou, Xiamen, Zhangzhou receiving the worst damage of the storm. Throughout the province, 67 people were killed and 31 other people were injured,[13] many seriously,[14] while 126,610 ha of crops were damaged.[13] Most of the casualties in the province occurred due to collapsed homes.[14]

In the neighboring province of Zhejiang, 28 others died and 71 were injured. There, the storm flooded 126,610 ha of crops and destroyed 700 homes. A highway tunnel in Huangyan County collapsed, burying at least 12 people, six of whom were rescued.[12]
Nationwide, 4,900 dwellings were demolished, 102 people sustained injuries, and 122 fatalities occurred.[1]
Throughout Hong Kong, there were no deaths or damages.[7]

Time_Annotation: Steadily organizing, the disturbance became a tropical depression on June 27, moving to the northwest due to a nearby ridge. Due to land interaction, Rumbia quickly weakened into a low-pressure area on July 2 and dissipated soon after.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: On June 28, the disturbance strengthened into Tropical Storm Rumbia, and the next day made its first landfall on Eastern Samar in the Philippines. The storm weakened slightly before moving ashore the Leizhou Peninsula in China late that day.
Main_Event_Annotation: On June 28, the disturbance strengthened into Tropical Storm Rumbia, and on July 1 it resumed strengthening to a peak of 95 km/h (60 mph) as a severe tropical storm, indicating its classification under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Upon landfall in the Philippines, Rumbia caused extensive flooding across multiple islands, and power outages resulted from the heavy rain and strong winds.

Time_Annotation: A broad circulation formed early on October 31. On November 1, the JMA reported that it was upgraded to a tropical depression about 280 km (175 mi) to the south of Palau. On November 2, the tropical depression weakened into a low-pressure area. On November 3, the system regenerated into a tropical depression and the JTWC issued a Tropical Cyclone Formation Alert. On November 4, Wilma weakened and spawned a waterspout that caused minor damage. On November 6, the system impacted Vietnam before becoming a remnant low late on November 7. Then on November 8, the remnants continued to move west, affecting Myanmar and later crossing the Malay Peninsula into the Bay of Bengal.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm impacted northern Mindanao (in the Philippines), impacted Vietnam on November 6, and affected Myanmar on November 8.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was upgraded to a tropical depression, later regenerated and prompted a Tropical Cyclone Formation Alert, and was named Wilma by PAGASA, indicating it is a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: On November 4, Wilma weakened and spawned a waterspout that caused minor damage, highlighting wind as the primary hazard.

Time_Annotation: The article states: 'Haiyan originated from an area of low pressure several hundred kilometers east-southeast of Pohnpei in the Federated States of Micronesia on November 2.' and later, 'Haiyan was last noted as a tropical depression by the JMA the following day.'
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text mentions the origin near Pohnpei in the Federated States of Micronesia, the storm passing over Kayangel in Palau, making landfall in the Philippines at Guiuan, Eastern Samar, striking northern Vietnam, and eventually degenerating over southern China.
Main_Event_Annotation: The description details the system evolving from a tropical disturbance into a tropical depression, then a tropical storm and eventually a typhoon, which classifies the event as a Tropical Storm/Cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The article cites extreme wind intensities (e.g., one-minute sustained winds of 315 km/h and landfall wind speeds of 305 km/h), indicating wind as the primary hazard.

Time_Annotation: On November 2, the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) began monitoring a broad low-pressure area about 425 km east-southeast of Pohnpei; Development continued throughout November 7, and at times, mesovortices were apparent in the typhoon's eye.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text notes the system was located east-southeast of Pohnpei (in the Federated States of Micronesia), the eye passed over the island of Kayangel in Palau, and the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) assigned the storm the local name Yolanda as it approached their area of responsibility.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was first classified as a tropical depression, then upgraded to a tropical storm (and later typhoon and super typhoon status) with the name Haiyan, clearly indicating a tropical storm/cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The report highlights rapid intensification with one-minute sustained winds reaching 165 km/h (105 mph), emphasizing the wind hazard associated with this tropical cyclone.

Time_Annotation: The origins of Typhoon Durian can be traced to a tropical disturbance that developed near Chuuk State in the Federated States of Micronesia on November 23. The remnants continued generally westward across the Bay and later dissipated on December 9 off the coast of Andhra Pradesh, India.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text notes that the disturbance developed near Chuuk State in the Federated States of Micronesia on November 23, tracked toward the Philippines (with multiple landfalls in regions such as northern Albay Province, Quezon, and Marinduque), paralleled the Vietnamese coastline, made landfall in Surat Thani Province, Thailand, and finally dissipated off the coast of Andhra Pradesh, India.
Main_Event_Annotation: The article describes the system being classified sequentially as a tropical depression, tropical storm (when the JMA named it Durian), and eventually a typhoon, indicating that it falls under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Numerous details in the text emphasize extreme wind conditions including sustained winds of 120 km/h to 260 km/h and gusts peaking at 320 km/h, demonstrating that high winds were a primary hazard of the event.

Time_Annotation: The remnants of Hurricane Ilsa interacted with a mid-level trough to produce a new low-level circulation on August 31, about 930 miles (1,500 km) northeast of Hawaii. Early on September 5, the cyclone became extratropical in the Gulf of Alaska, while located about 315 miles (510 km) southwest of Juneau, Alaska.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Early on September 5, the cyclone became extratropical in the Gulf of Alaska, while located about 315 miles (510 km) southwest of Juneau, Alaska. On the same day, the circulation was rapidly absorbed by the frontal system, and the remnants quickly reached the coast of British Columbia. The remnants of the storm turned southeastward, and the low was last tracked definitively to a point north of Montana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Its track over warmer waters caused the storm to transition into a tropical storm on September 2, by which time the convection organized into rainbands. Around that time, the storm developed an eye in the center of the convection, suggesting that it intensified into a hurricane late on September 3.
Hazards_Annotation: A nearby ship reported sustained winds of 63 mph (102 km/h), while another nearby ship reported a pressure of 1003 mbar (29.6 inHg), with a 3-hour tendency increase of 13.5 mbar (0.40 inHg), suggesting a minimum pressure of under 990 mbar. The storm also experienced strong wind shear as it weakened after maintaining hurricane status.

Time_Annotation: During the second week of October, an unusually large, monsoon‐like lower‐level circulation and disturbed weather developed over the Caribbean Sea. By October 13, a broad area of low pressure developed and persisted about 150 miles southeast of Jamaica. By late on October 15, the system was defined well enough for the National Hurricane Center to designate it as Tropical Depression Twenty-Four.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The article states that by October 13 a broad area of low pressure developed about 150 miles (240 km) southeast of Jamaica, indicating that Jamaica was affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: The National Hurricane Center mentioned that the system could ultimately become a hurricane and later designated it as Tropical Depression Twenty-Four, which places the event under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The article notes that continued reconnaissance flights reported peak winds of about 30 mph (48 km/h), evidencing wind as the primary hazard.

Time_Annotation: On July 6, a tropical wave entered the Northeastern Pacific Ocean. An area of low pressure developed and began to show signs of organization on July 9. The disturbance was designated a tropical depression around 12:00 UTC on July 10 while located about 650 mi (1,045 km) south-southeast of Baja California Sur. The storm became more organized and was named Tropical Storm Enrique 24 hours later as it tracked west-northwest. The cyclone instead peaked with winds of 65 mph (105 km/h) early on July 12, and the storm degenerated into a remnant low around 00:00 UTC on July 14 and continued to move west before dissipating three days later.

Main_Event_Annotation: It was explicitly named Tropical Storm Enrique, indicating its classification under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The cyclone peaked with winds of 65 mph (105 km/h), highlighting wind as the primary hazard associated with this event.
